statement: Let P be the set of ordered pairs (i,j) of integers such that 0 <= i < len(nums), 0 <= j < len(nums), i != j, and the byte-list concatenation nums[i] ++ nums[j] equals target. Here nums[i] ++ nums[j] = target means len(nums[i]) + len(nums[j]) = len(target), for every 0 <= k < len(nums[i]) we have nums[i][k] = target[k], and for every 0 <= k < len(nums[j]) we have nums[j][k] = target[len(nums[i]) + k]. Whenever num_of_pairs(nums, target) returns a result r, r is the number of elements of P, i.e. the number of ordered index pairs (i,j) with i != j whose concatenated digit strings equal target.
preconditions: len(nums) is an integer with 2 <= len(nums) <= 100; for every i with 0 <= i < len(nums), nums[i] is a byte list with 1 <= len(nums[i]) <= 100 and every byte nums[i][k] for 0 <= k < len(nums[i]) satisfies 48 <= nums[i][k] <= 57; for every i, if len(nums[i]) > 1 then nums[i][0] != 48 (no leading zero); target is a byte list with 2 <= len(target) <= 100 and every byte target[k] for 0 <= k < len(target) satisfies 48 <= target[k] <= 57, and target[0] != 48 (no leading zero, since len(target) >= 2).

statement: num_of_pairs(nums, target) returns a result r; equivalently, the call does not fail, panic, overflow, or access outside the bounds of nums or target.
